question: Which learning principles could let an AI adapt to tasks and distributions not seen during training, and does the evidence establish rich features, predictive disentanglement, and memory-based inference-time learning as scalable answers?

key_findings.claim: The thesis offers a coherent three-part agenda for open-world learning: prepare redundant features, organize prediction into reusable components, and adapt at inference through memory rather than parameter updates.
key_findings.evidence: The introduction names rich features, disentangled representation, and inference-time learning as the respective analogues of a large toolbox, an organized toolbox, and a tool-savvy hand. The closing chapter connects them: rich features ease optimization, disentanglement supports reuse, and both are intended to make memory-based few-example adaptation viable.

key_findings.claim: The rich-feature theorem is much narrower than the chapter's broad conclusion that single-episode i.i.d. training lacks motivation to construct rich features regardless of model and data size.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2.1.6 concerns unconstrained global minimizers of the same expected-risk problem and defines information through an optimal convex-loss linear probe on that same distribution. The text itself then acknowledges that real networks do not truly optimize this idealized expected error. The theorem neither analyzes SGD nor proves that practical training deletes features useful under an unknown shifted distribution.

anchors.section: 2.1.4 Optimization dynamics and 2.2 Learning rich features

key_findings.claim: Concatenation and Bonsai provide credible evidence that diverse training episodes can improve transfer, but the experiments do not isolate feature richness from extra optimization, model topology, and training compute.
key_findings.evidence: Cat10 reaches 49.65 on iNaturalist18, 79.61 on CIFAR-100, and 93.75 on CIFAR-10 linear probes after ImageNet training, exceeding displayed widened and multi-branch baselines. On Camelyon17, frozen two-round Bonsai yields 78.2-79.5 accuracy across ERM and invariant penalties, whereas the ordinary ERM initialization is lower and more variable. Cat uses up to 20 independently trained networks, while Bonsai adds discovery and distillation episodes; neither comparison is training-compute matched. The appendix also says ColoredMNIST hyperparameters were chosen by peeking at test performance.

key_findings.claim: Very-large dropout is a simple, repeatable fine-tuning intervention with modest OOD gains, but the proposed mechanism of preserving rich pretrained features is inferred rather than measured.
key_findings.evidence: Applying dropout at the penultimate layer during fine-tuning raises the four-dataset ResNet average from 72.0 for ERM and 72.9 for the best displayed averaging or ensemble baseline to 74.0; for ViT-L/16 it raises 70.5-70.6 to 71.4. Rates near 90% work consistently, whereas scratch training fails and stronger augmentation-pretraining produces larger gains. The study does not quantify representation diversity, feature survival, or causal mediation, and its main table reports no uncertainty intervals.

key_findings.claim: Predictive disentanglement is compellingly illustrated on the three-moons toy problem but is not established as an identifiable or measurable property of the language models.
key_findings.evidence: A 54-parameter, three-head memory network learns one periodic component per head and predicts after observing the longest individual period rather than the combined least-common-multiple period. For BabiStories language modeling, however, the thesis reports loss and downstream behavior without a factor-recovery metric, intervention study, head-specialization statistic, or theorem ensuring independent memories align with independent generative factors.

key_findings.claim: Two mathematical details weaken the theoretical presentation of the associative-memory mechanism without invalidating the trainable architecture.
key_findings.evidence: Expanding the equal-norm Gaussian kernel exp(-beta ||k-k_i||^2) produces a similarity term exp(2 beta k dot k_i), while Equation 3.8 prints exp(beta k dot k_i); a learned bandwidth can absorb this factor. The accompanying Nadaraya-Watson footnote states convergence for beta=sqrt(n) without dimension, density, smoothness, or bandwidth conditions, so it cannot support a universal high-dimensional consistency claim.

key_findings.claim: The original Memory Mosaics result supports parity with a GPT-2-like transformer on one synthetic language corpus and better selected context use, not a general superiority result.
key_findings.evidence: At sufficient depth, training and validation losses on Mixtral-generated BabiStories are described as indistinguishable. The Memory Mosaic becomes better after roughly 50 positions on Simple English Wikipedia and performs strongly on RegBench, with transformer-tuned hyperparameters copied to both. These are medium-scale experiments on synthetic pretraining data and two selected OOD or in-context tests, with no measured disentanglement in language.

key_findings.claim: Memory Mosaics v2 matches the transformer on common benchmarks and is substantially better on two RULER document-QA tasks, but the comparison changes resources and uses a weak long-context control.
key_findings.evidence: After 32k fine-tuning, both large models average 52.2 over 19 common benchmarks. On RULER at 32k, the 9.9B, 18.9B-FLOP-per-token Memory Mosaic scores 53.4 versus 41.1 for the 8.8B, 16.7B-FLOP transformer. The 4k-pretrained tables leave the transformer unevaluated beyond its trained length, and the baseline is a vanilla RoPE transformer rather than current sparse, recurrent, retrieval, or test-time-memory systems. Removing long-term memory also reduces both parameters and FLOPs, so its ablation is not isolated.

key_findings.claim: The claim of almost no task-specific prior or hyperparameter choice in inference-time classification is inconsistent with the reported evaluation procedure.
key_findings.evidence: For every shot count, the study evaluates four prompt strategies made from delimiter and shuffle choices and selects the best, without identifying a separate prompt-selection split. Its fine-tuning comparison also imports published RoBERTa results from different models and protocols: Memory Mosaics v2 scores 89.5, 63.0, and 31.4 on Banking77, TACRED, and GoEmotion versus reported fine-tuning scores of 93.7, 70.1, and 48.2. The method uses fewer labeled examples, but this is not a controlled algorithm comparison and the prompt selection is itself task-specific prior.

key_findings.claim: The strongest thesis-level novelty is the synthesis and the large Memory Mosaics v2 experiment; most component methods substantially overlap the author's prior papers, and the field-level label of a new inference-time-learning paradigm is too broad.
key_findings.evidence: The rich-representation experiments, Bonsai, very-large dropout, and original Memory Mosaics correspond closely to the author's ICML 2023, ICML 2022, arXiv 2024, and ICLR 2025 papers. Chapter 4 introduces the scaled v2 architecture and experiments, later posted separately as Memory Mosaics at scale. Long before this thesis, memory networks, kNN language models, Memorizing Transformers, in-context learning, fast weights, and test-time training already adapted computation or memory during inference.

anchors.section: 2.3 Case study: rich feature in invariant learning

method.core_idea: Prepare a broad set of linearly usable features before distribution shift, encourage independent memory heads to decompose fast prediction, and use those features through nonparametric associative memories when new examples arrive at inference time.
method.mechanism: The rich-feature chapter combines representations from independent runs, discovers complementary predictors with Bonsai and distills them, or applies very high penultimate-layer dropout during fine-tuning. Memory Mosaics train key and future-peeking value extractors around causal Gaussian-kernel memories; quick-learning pressure is defined through early prediction loss. Version 2 adds context-dependent recurrent keys, adaptive bandwidth, separate short- and long-term contextual memories, a persistent feed-forward memory, and an optional bag-of-next-tokens objective.
assumptions: Unseen tasks will reuse features that can be prepared from the training distributions and exposed to a simple downstream learner.
Diversity across random seeds, discovery rounds, or dropout corresponds to useful semantic feature richness rather than merely larger effective compute or ensembles.
Independent associative-memory heads trained for rapid prediction will discover reusable independent subtasks without explicit factor supervision.
Gaussian-kernel similarity remains statistically and computationally useful in learned high-dimensional key spaces.
Storing all prior key-value pairs is acceptable, or approximate retrieval can reduce cost without erasing the measured learning behavior.
The chosen benchmarks, prompts, parameter counts, training tokens, and FLOPs provide a fair proxy for broad open-world adaptation.

techniques.role: Concatenate penultimate representations from independent training episodes to retain redundant transfer features.
Alternate complementary-feature discovery with pseudo-label distillation into one rich representation.
Apply roughly 90% dropout at the penultimate layer while fine-tuning a pretrained backbone.
Implement causal associative retrieval as normalized Gaussian Nadaraya-Watson regression over stored key-value pairs.
Use the area under the per-position prediction-loss curve as pressure for components that become useful from few observations.
Scale kernel sharpness as a learned function of the number of stored examples.
Build context-sensitive recurrent key features rather than fixed leaky averages.
Separate short-term positional memory, long-term permutation-invariant contextual memory, and persistent parametric memory.
Add unordered prediction of the next token block to provide learning signals for context-length extrapolation.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet-supervised ResNet-50 representations transferred by linear probing to iNaturalist18, CIFAR-100, and CIFAR-10.
evaluations.result: Cat10 obtains 49.65, 79.61, and 93.75 on the three targets.
evaluations.baseline: The displayed parameter-near wide or multi-branch single-training baselines reach at most 41.89, 74.81, and 92.13 respectively, but Cat10 uses ten independent training runs.

evaluations.setting: WILDS Camelyon17 with five seeds, multiple invariant objectives, and IID or OOD tuning.
evaluations.result: Frozen two-round Bonsai ranges from 77.8 to 79.5 across ERM, IRMv1, vREx, and CLOvE.
evaluations.baseline: Ordinary ERM initialization ranges from 66.6 to 71.7 with much larger standard deviations; invariant penalties add little once the two-round representation is frozen.

evaluations.setting: DomainBed VLCS, OfficeHome, PACS, and TerraIncognita fine-tuning with ResNet-50 or ViT-L/16.
evaluations.metric: Average OOD accuracy after IID hyperparameter selection
evaluations.result: Very-large dropout obtains 74.0 for ResNet-50 and 71.4 for ViT-L/16.
evaluations.baseline: ERM obtains 72.0 and 70.5; the best displayed ordinary single-run averaging or ensemble obtains 72.9 and 70.6.

evaluations.setting: Original medium-scale Memory Mosaics and GPT-2-like transformers trained on BabiStories, then tested on Simple English Wikipedia and RegBench.
evaluations.metric: Language-model loss and in-context benchmark score
evaluations.result: Deep models have essentially indistinguishable BabiStories loss; Memory Mosaics becomes better after about 50 Simple-Wikipedia positions and leads the displayed RegBench comparison.
evaluations.baseline: A parameter-matched transformer using the same transformer-tuned hyperparameter space.

evaluations.setting: Large models trained on one trillion tokens and fine-tuned from 4k to 32k context, evaluated over 19 conventional language benchmarks.
evaluations.result: Memory Mosaics v2 Large and Transformer Large both obtain 52.2 after context extension.
evaluations.baseline: At 4k, Transformer Large scores 53.6 and Memory Mosaics v2 Large scores 52.1.

evaluations.setting: Two RULER multi-document question-answering tasks at 4k-64k sequence lengths.
evaluations.result: After 32k context fine-tuning, Memory Mosaics v2 Large scores 58.9, 55.5, 54.9, and 53.4 at 4k, 8k, 16k, and 32k, and 46.4 at 64k.
evaluations.baseline: Transformer Large scores 51.2, 48.8, 44.7, and 41.1 through 32k and is not evaluated at 64k; it is smaller and uses about 13% fewer FLOPs per token.

evaluations.setting: Banking77, TACRED, and GoEmotion few-shot classification with semantic and anonymous labels.
evaluations.result: The Memory Mosaic curves generally improve with more shots and often exceed the matched transformer curves by over ten points on the selected prompt strategy.
evaluations.baseline: Four prompt variants are tried and the best is selected for each shot count; separately published fine-tuned RoBERTa models score higher but use more examples and different protocols.

evaluations.setting: RULER question answering with next-token versus next-token plus bag-of-next-64-token pretraining at 4k context.
evaluations.metric: 4k and 8k accuracy before and after 32k fine-tuning
evaluations.result: The extra objective raises the 4k-pretrained model from 59.3 to 61.3 at 4k and from 48.8 to 57.6 at 8k; 32k fine-tuning then changes the latter by only 0.8 points.
evaluations.baseline: Only Memory Mosaics v2 is ablated; the transformer is not trained with the same multi-token objective.

limitations: Author-stated: exact memory retrieval has O(n) inference time and memory in the number of stored examples; the proposed fuzzy or hierarchical remedies are future work.

Reviewer inference: the thesis does not operationalize open-world AI as a falsifiable end-to-end benchmark; it aggregates transfer, OOD, synthetic disentanglement, long-context QA, and in-context classification proxies.

Reviewer inference: the main rich-feature comparisons add independent training episodes, architecture branches, discovery phases, or distillation, so training compute and optimization are not controlled.
Reviewer inference: ColoredMNIST hyperparameters are selected by inspecting test performance, compromising its use as held-out OOD evidence.
Reviewer inference: predictive disentanglement has no identifiability guarantee or quantitative language-model evaluation beyond a hand-auditable toy system.
Reviewer inference: Memory Mosaics v2 and its transformer differ in parameters and FLOPs, while the long-term-memory ablation changes both capacity and computation.
Reviewer inference: the large-scale data mixture is described only by broad source categories, preventing a contamination, licensing, deduplication, or exact replication audit.
Reviewer inference: long-context evidence is concentrated in two RULER QA tasks and excludes direct modern memory, sparse-attention, retrieval, and test-time-training competitors.
Reviewer inference: prompt-strategy selection, absent uncertainty intervals on many curves, and cross-paper fine-tuning numbers weaken the classification comparison.
Reviewer inference: no sequential continual-learning benchmark tests the claim that local memory updates avoid negative interference across many evolving tasks.
failure_modes: A pretraining distribution may omit the features needed by a genuinely novel task, leaving no rich representation for a linear probe or memory to reuse.
Repeated training and feature concatenation can scale cost and representation width faster than their transfer benefit.
Bonsai discovery can amplify errors in its correct-versus-misclassified split or distill brittle pseudo-label features; the third Camelyon round already degrades performance.
Very high dropout can destroy optimization when the starting representation is not sufficiently pretrained or when the downstream boundary requires coordinated features.
Independent memory heads can collapse to redundant predictors or learn a decomposition unrelated to causal or reusable factors.
Kernel retrieval can suffer the curse of dimensionality, bandwidth miscalibration, near-duplicate collisions, or spurious high-similarity memories.
Storing every key-value pair makes long sessions quadratically expensive over a full sequence and can retain stale, private, adversarial, or contradictory information.
Approximate retrieval may remove exactly the rare examples on which the claimed few-shot adaptation depends.
Selecting the best prompt on evaluation data can turn apparent inference-time learning into benchmark-specific model selection.
Context-length gains on retrieval-heavy synthetic tasks may fail to transfer to global reasoning, conflict resolution, temporal updates, or noisy real conversations.
reusable_insights: Separate open-world learning into representation preparation, factor organization, and deployment-time adaptation; each stage needs its own measurable contract.
Evaluate a representation by what a deliberately simple learner can extract after a shift, not only by training-distribution accuracy.
The area under a learning curve is a useful objective when rapid benefit from the first few examples matters more than asymptotic accuracy.
Distinguish persistent training knowledge, storage of new facts, and acquisition of new input-output rules when evaluating memory architectures.
A frozen rich representation can be a diagnostic: if sophisticated invariant penalties stop helping, representation construction may be the true bottleneck.
Adaptive kernel bandwidth is a principled way to couple retrieval sharpness to memory size, but its statistical assumptions must be tested in the learned key geometry.
Multi-token future objectives can reveal extrapolation parameters that next-token loss under a short context cannot identify.
Open-world claims need compute-matched baselines, held-out selection protocols, and explicit human-prior accounting in addition to headline benchmark gains.
open_questions: Can predictive disentanglement be given an identifiability theorem or intervention-based metric that scales beyond a periodic toy system?
Does very-large dropout measurably preserve more transferable features, or are its gains explained by conventional regularization and optimization effects?

What is the Pareto frontier of Memory Mosaics v2, Titans, TTT, MIRAS, ATLAS, Trellis, retrieval-augmented transformers, and sparse attention under equal parameters, tokens, FLOPs, latency, and memory?
Can sublinear or bounded memory preserve rare-event recall, support deletion and conflict resolution, and avoid privacy leakage?
How does Memory Mosaics v2 behave on realistic continual task streams with updates, reversals, distractors, and measured catastrophic forgetting?
Do the long-context and in-context gains persist with a held-out prompt-selection set, repeated trials, contamination controls, and strong current transformer recipes?
How should feature richness be quantified independently of downstream accuracy, width, and the number of training episodes?
Which training objectives provide reliable context-length extrapolation across retrieval, reasoning, summarization, and multimodal streams rather than only RULER QA?
What human knowledge is actually required to select the memory design, prompt serialization, bandwidth rule, and task interface for a new domain?
Can the three-part agenda be tested on an end-to-end open-world protocol where tasks arrive sequentially and evaluation criteria were not used to design the learner?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning useful representations for shifting tasks and distributions
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang and Bottou already introduce the linear-probe richness framework and Cat experiments; the thesis integrates that work into a broader agenda rather than establishing a new rich-feature result from scratch.

competitive_landscape.title: Rich Feature Construction for the Optimization-Generalization Dilemma
competitive_landscape.difference: This ICML paper already presents RFC/Bonsai and its ColoredMNIST and Camelyon evidence; the thesis mainly reframes it as one implementation of the rich-feature principle.

competitive_landscape.title: Fine-tuning with Very Large Dropout
competitive_landscape.difference: The same authors' preprint contains the very-large-dropout method and DomainBed experiments reproduced in Chapter 2, limiting the thesis-specific novelty of that case study.

competitive_landscape.title: Memory Mosaics
competitive_landscape.difference: The ICLR 2025 paper already introduces kernel-regression memory units, predictive disentanglement, the three-moons demonstration, and medium-scale language results; the thesis adds the v2 scaling chapter and cross-principle synthesis.

competitive_landscape.title: Memory Mosaics at scale
competitive_landscape.difference: This later preprint presents the 10B, one-trillion-token Memory Mosaics v2 work as a standalone paper, closely matching Chapter 4 and making the thesis's main new empirical contribution independently citable.

competitive_landscape.title: No One Representation to Rule Them All: Overlapping Features of Training Methods
competitive_landscape.difference: Gontijo-Lopes et al. diversify training methods and show overlapping, non-superset feature sets and unusually strong ensembles; this is a broader diversity intervention than Cat's random-seed-only construction and directly motivates richer diversification controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Model Ratatouille: Recycling Diverse Models for Out-of-Distribution Generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Ratatouille reuses diverse auxiliary fine-tunings as target initializations and averages the resulting weights, achieving strong DomainBed performance without concatenated inference width; it tests a more deployment-efficient route to diversity than Cat.

competitive_landscape.title: Challenging Common Assumptions in the Unsupervised Learning of Disentangled Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Locatello et al. prove that unsupervised disentanglement needs inductive biases and show model selection and downstream utility cannot be assumed; those concerns apply directly because the thesis does not quantify or identify predictive disentanglement beyond its toy example.

competitive_landscape.title: Memorizing Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Wu et al. attach approximate k-nearest-neighbor memory of recent internal key-value pairs to a transformer and demonstrate test-time acquisition across text, code, and theorem data, predating the thesis's broad inference-time-memory novelty claim.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States
competitive_landscape.difference: TTT layers make the recurrent hidden state a learned model updated by self-supervised gradient steps, providing linear sequence complexity and bounded state rather than storing every contextual key-value pair.

competitive_landscape.title: Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time
competitive_landscape.difference: Titans combines attention as short-term memory with an online-learned neural long-term memory and reports language, reasoning, genomics, time-series, and multi-million-token results; it is a direct missing comparator for the v2 three-level-memory claim.

competitive_landscape.title: It's All Connected: A Journey Through Test-Time Memorization, Attentional Bias, Retention, and Online Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: MIRAS treats sequence architectures as combinations of memory form, internal objective, retention, and update rule, yielding several parallelizable memory models; it offers a broader design taxonomy and bounded-memory alternatives to exact Memory Mosaics retrieval.

competitive_landscape.title: ATLAS: Learning to Optimally Memorize the Context at Test Time
competitive_landscape.difference: ATLAS optimizes a high-capacity long-term memory over current and past tokens and reports improvements over Titans through ten-million-token BABILong contexts, directly extending the scaling axis that the thesis tests only to 64k.

competitive_landscape.title: TRELLIS: Learning to Compress Key-Value Memory in Attention Models
competitive_landscape.difference: TRELLIS learns a fixed-size, recursively updated key-value memory with test-time gradient descent, directly targeting the unbounded storage and retrieval cost that the thesis leaves to future approximate search.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The thesis presents three necessary learning principles for open-world AI, introduces predictive disentanglement and Memory Mosaics v2, and describes inference-time learning as a new paradigm that can outperform transformers on acquiring new knowledge and tasks.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The thesis unifies four earlier lines of the author's work, adds a three-level 9.9B Memory Mosaics v2 trained on one trillion tokens, evaluates persistent knowledge, new knowledge, and in-context rule learning separately, and studies an extra future-token objective for length extrapolation.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The integration is intellectually useful and Memory Mosaics v2 is a substantive new thesis contribution. However, Cat, Bonsai, very-large dropout, and original Memory Mosaics substantially reproduce prior papers; inference-time adaptation through context, memory, retrieval, fast weights, and test-time optimization predates the thesis. The evidence supports promising methods on selected proxies, not the necessity of the three principles, identifiable language disentanglement, or a scalable field-wide replacement for transformers.

reviewer_notes: Read all 149 PDF pages against the pinned extraction. Pages 2 and 113 had no usable extracted text; I rendered them and verified that they contain only the copyright notice and an appendix divider, and no finding cites them. I also rendered and inspected the principal architecture figures, attention plots, equations, transfer and OOD tables, three-moons curves, 19-task benchmark table, RULER tables, in-context-learning plots, and appendix ablations. Primary arXiv, OpenReview, and PMLR records for direct predecessors and current competitors were checked on 2026-08-23. Numerical claims distinguish author-reported results from reviewer inference; the thesis is assessed as a multi-study synthesis rather than treated as one controlled experiment.
